paper_metadata.title: Quantum Speedups for Derivative Pricing: Beyond Black-Scholes

summary: The paper proves that quantum Monte Carlo integration using amplitude estimation can achieve an end‑to‑end quadratic speedup (sampling complexity ~O(1/ε) vs classical O(1/ε²)) for pricing derivatives under several stochastic models including CIR and a restricted multi‑asset Heston model. The algorithms require poly(T,d,log(1/ε)) gate overhead and O(poly(T)) qubits, with a further result showing quantum MLMC achieves eO(poly(T,d)·σ₀/ε) complexity using a quantum Milstein sampler for bipartite‑correlated processes.

experiments.description: Theoretical quantum Monte Carlo pricing of path-independent and path-dependent derivatives over geometric Brownian motion (GBM/Black-Scholes), using quantum amplitude estimation with discrete qsample preparation and improved discretization analysis.

algorithm.variant: quantum Monte Carlo integration (QMCI) for derivative pricing over GBM

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Discrete qsample over a truncated and discretized path grid; payoff encoded into an ancilla via controlled rotations. For GBM, path increments are independent Gaussians and can be loaded as a tensor product of Gaussian states.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate E[f(\u1d4ebX)] for a derivative payoff f over a GBM path process \u1d4ebX.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Truncation to [−R,R] and left-endpoint Riemann discretization; no QUBO/Ising formulation.

problem_instance.description: Multi-asset GBM / Black-Scholes derivative pricing, including path-dependent payoffs such as Asian options.

dataset_specification.description: Stochastic process model rather than empirical dataset.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Truncate continuous distributions, discretize each dimension on a uniform grid, and load Gaussian primitives.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Asymptotic resource analysis; no numerical benchmark runs reported.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical truncation/discretization analysis; coherent arithmetic for payoff evaluation.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Amplitude estimation to recover the price estimate.

speedup_claims.conditions: for quantum Monte Carlo integration with discrete qsample preparation; end-to-end resource analysis for GBM/Black-Scholes path-independent and path-dependent pricing
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper emphasizes that the black-box quadratic speedup must be combined with state-preparation and discretization analysis; the result is theoretical and asymptotic.

speedup_claims.conditions: asymptotic pricing of GBM/Black-Scholes derivatives with amplitude estimation and the stated truncation/discretization assumptions
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper is theoretical and reports asymptotic resource bounds only; no hardware runs.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: eO(σ/ϵ) sampling complexity; end-to-end gate complexity eO(poly(d, log(1/ϵ)) · sqrt(Var(f(\u1d4ebX))/ϵ))
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(Var(f(\u1d4ebX))/ϵ^2) samples for Monte Carlo integration

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires fault‑tolerant quantum computers capable of implementing QMCI circuits with poly(d,log(1/ε)) overhead and amplitude estimation iterations.
limiting_factors: Only quadratic speedup from amplitude estimation
Large overhead from coherent arithmetic and distribution loading

notes: The paper is theoretical and reports asymptotic resource bounds rather than experimental hardware runs.
The paper discusses asymptotic quadratic speedup for QMCI but presents no empirical implementation.

experiments.description: Theoretical quantum pricing over the Cox–Ingersoll–Ross (CIR) process using fast-forwarding, primitive distribution loading (Gaussian and chi-square), and amplitude estimation.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Path increments are loaded from standard Gaussian and central chi-square primitives; CIR transition is recursively computed as c(y + (z + sqrt(βv))^2).
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate E[f(\u1d4ebV)] for a derivative payoff f over a CIR path process \u1d4ebV.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Truncation of Gaussian and chi-square primitives; recursive coherent arithmetic for the CIR transition; no QUBO/Ising formulation.

problem_instance.description: Derivative pricing over a single CIR process, including path-dependent Lipschitz payoffs.

dataset_specification.description: Stochastic process model rather than empirical dataset.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Truncate Gaussian and chi-square primitives; discretize on a uniform grid; recursively compute the CIR path.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Asymptotic resource analysis; no numerical benchmark runs reported.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical truncation and discretization analysis; recursive fixed-point arithmetic for CIR updates.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Amplitude estimation to recover the price estimate.

results.value: O(T log(N)) for the loaded state; O(T log(BTN)) total during preparation
O(T^2 log^2(N) log(T) + T(b+r)log(N)log(BTb/ε) + log^3(BTbN) + N_f)
O(T^2 log^2(N) log(T) + T(b+r)log(N)log(BTb/ϵ) + log^3(BTbN) + N_f)

speedup_claims.conditions: single-asset CIR with fast-forwarding; piecewise-linear B-Lipschitz payoff; η ≥ 5; truncation/discretization controlled
speedup_claims.caveats: The theorem is asymptotic and relies on recursive coherent arithmetic for the CIR transition and on primitive loading of Gaussian and chi-square distributions.

speedup_claims.conditions: CIR pricing with fast-forwarding, truncated Gaussian and chi-square primitives, and amplitude estimation
speedup_claims.caveats: Asymptotic analysis only; no numerical benchmark runs reported.

complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical Monte Carlo integration requires O(Var(f(X))/ε^2) samples; quantum algorithm achieves eO(poly(T,B)/ε) gate complexity.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires fault‑tolerant circuits implementing recursive CIR fast‑forwarding and amplitude estimation with precision ε.
limiting_factors: Large qubit counts proportional to T log(1/ε)

notes: The paper provides asymptotic resource estimates only; no device or simulator is named.
Theorem 6.3 explicitly claims an end‑to‑end quadratic asymptotic speedup for CIR pricing.

experiments.description: Theoretical quantum pricing over a multi-asset Heston model with asset-asset correlations only, using fast-forwarding, loading of CIR integrals and conditional distributions, and amplitude estimation.

algorithm.variant: QMCI with fast-forwardable multi-asset Heston model

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Path increments include Gaussian, chi-square, and conditional CIR-integral primitives; Heston price path is reconstructed recursively and then payoff-encoded.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate E[f(\u1d4ebS)] for a derivative payoff f over a multi-asset Heston path process \u1d4ebS.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Truncation of all primitive distributions; lower-endpoint truncation near zero for the CIR integral; no QUBO/Ising formulation.

problem_instance.description: Multi-asset Heston pricing with asset-asset correlations only; path-dependent Lipschitz payoffs.

dataset_specification.description: Stochastic process model rather than empirical dataset.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Load CIR processes, standard Gaussians, and conditional CIR-integral distributions; discretize and truncate all primitives.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Asymptotic resource analysis; no numerical benchmark runs reported.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical truncation/discretization analysis; recursive arithmetic for Heston path construction.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Amplitude estimation to recover the price estimate.

results.value: O(dT log(N)) for the loaded state; O(poly(d,T,b,log(B))) total

speedup_claims.conditions: multi-asset Heston with asset-asset correlations only; piecewise-linear B-Lipschitz payoff; parameter constraints on Δ, κ, σ, ρ, and η_k ≥ 5; truncation/discretization controlled
speedup_claims.caveats: The result is for a restricted Heston variant (asset-asset correlations only) and is asymptotic; no hardware benchmark is reported.

speedup_claims.conditions: multi-asset Heston pricing with fast-forwardable CIR components, truncation of primitive distributions, and amplitude estimation
speedup_claims.caveats: No concrete hardware implementation; asymptotic resource analysis only.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: eO(poly(d, T, B)/ε) one‑ and two‑qubit gates with O(poly(T)) qubits for estimating derivative prices.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Not explicitly given as a separate theorem; implied Monte Carlo baseline is O(1/ϵ^2) sampling complexity

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires large fault‑tolerant quantum circuits implementing Heston fast‑forwarding with conditional CIR‑integral loading and amplitude estimation.
limiting_factors: Very large polynomial overhead in T and d

notes: The paper is theoretical and does not report a concrete hardware implementation.
Theorem 6.6 claims an end‑to‑end quadratic asymptotic speedup for the fast‑forwardable Heston model variant.

experiments.description: Theoretical quantum multi-level Monte Carlo (QMLMC) for approximate SDE simulation with bipartite correlations, using a quantum Milstein sampler and two-dimensional Lévy area loading.

algorithm.variant: quantum MLMC with Milstein scheme and quantum Lévy-area sampler

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Milstein-discretized SDE paths are coupled across MLMC levels; primitives are Gaussian increments and conditional two-dimensional Lévy areas.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate E[f(\u1d4ebX)] for a globally Lipschitz derivative payoff under approximate SDE simulation.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: MLMC telescoping estimator; truncation/discretization/distribution errors controlled separately; no QUBO/Ising formulation.

problem_instance.description: Globally Lipschitz derivative pricing for SDEs with bipartite correlations, including models requiring Lévy-area sampling.

dataset_specification.description: Stochastic process model rather than empirical dataset.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Construct coupled Milstein paths at multiple levels; load Gaussian and conditional Lévy-area primitives; truncate and discretize all primitives.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Asymptotic resource analysis; no numerical benchmark runs reported.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical MLMC coupling and Milstein discretization; primitive loading for Gaussian and Lévy-area distributions.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: MLMC telescoping sum and amplitude estimation.

speedup_claims.conditions: globally Lipschitz payoff; approximate SDE simulation with Milstein scheme; bipartite correlations; quantum MLMC framework; 0.99 success probability
speedup_claims.caveats: The result is restricted to bipartite correlations and relies on a quantum Milstein sampler with two-dimensional Lévy-area loading; the paper notes that arbitrary correlations remain open.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical Monte Carlo / classical MLMC with Euler-Maruyama
speedup_claims.conditions: globally Lipschitz SDEs with bipartite correlations, Milstein discretization, and quantum Lévy-area loading
speedup_claims.caveats: The theorem is asymptotic and assumes truncation/discretization/distribution errors are controlled separately.

complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical MLMC with Euler-Maruyama is O((σ0/ϵ)^2) in the globally Lipschitz setting; standard Monte Carlo is worse

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Fault‑tolerant implementation of quantum MLMC with Milstein discretization and efficient Lévy area sampling.
limiting_factors: Complex state preparation for Lévy areas
High polynomial overhead in dimension and time steps
No numerical resource estimates for practical instances

notes: This is a theoretical MLMC result; no experimental hardware or simulator is specified.
Theorem 7.2 provides an asymptotic quadratic speedup for QMLMC under bipartite correlation assumptions.

experiments.description: Theoretical use of quantum PDE solvers to prepare Fokker-Planck history states for derivative pricing, followed by analysis showing why this approach is not compatible with Monte Carlo pricing for path-dependent derivatives.

algorithm.variant: quantum linear-systems / Fokker-Planck PDE solver for state preparation

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Finite-difference discretization of the Fokker-Planck PDE into a linear system Bp=b; quantum linear systems algorithm used to prepare a history state over marginals.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Prepare a quantum state encoding the solution of the Fokker-Planck equation for an SDE marginal distribution.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Finite-difference discretization, upwind scheme, and linear-system solving; no QUBO/Ising formulation.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: B = block matrix built from I and M = I + LΔt

problem_instance.description: Fokker-Planck PDE state preparation for GBM/CIR marginals, analyzed as a potential subroutine for derivative pricing.
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Finite-difference discretization in space and time; upwind scheme for convection/diffusion terms.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Asymptotic resource analysis and no-go arguments; no numerical benchmark runs reported.

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Amplitude amplification / inner-product estimation discussed as barriers for pricing.

results.unit: queries to state and matrix oracles

speedup_claims.conditions: finite-difference discretization of the Fokker-Planck equation; quantum linear systems algorithm; efficient state and matrix oracles; not used as a compatible subroutine for Monte Carlo pricing of path-dependent derivatives
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper’s main conclusion is negative for pricing: history states from the PDE solver are insufficient for path-dependent payoffs, and the ℓ2/ℓ1 normalization mismatch plus condition-number dependence limit usefulness.

speedup_claims.conditions: finite-difference Fokker-Planck state preparation with HHL-style linear-system solving
speedup_claims.caveats: This is presented as a proposed subroutine and barrier analysis, not an experimental benchmark; the paper also notes incompatibility with Monte Carlo pricing for path-dependent derivatives.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(κ log(1/ϵ)) queries to state and matrix oracles; overall O(poly(log(T), log(n), d) · κ log(1/ϵ)) gates
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Not given as a single theorem; classical PDE solvers suffer curse of dimensionality

notes: This is a proposed subroutine and barrier analysis, not an experimental benchmark.

experiments.description: Quantum multi‑level Monte Carlo (QMLMC) derivative pricing for SDEs with bipartite correlations using a quantum Milstein sampler and a quantum algorithm for sampling two‑dimensional Lévy areas.

algorithm.variant: Quantum MLMC with Milstein scheme and quantum Lévy area sampler

key_results: Quantum algorithm estimates derivative prices to ε additive error using eO(poly(T,d)·σ0/ε) one‑ and two‑qubit gates.
End‑to‑end quadratic speedup relative to classical MLMC for globally‑Lipschitz payoffs when the SDE has bipartite correlations.
Requires quantum sampling of (d,2) Lévy areas and Milstein‑level discretization accuracy.
